sections.b: With Proverbs 10:1 the book changes form. In place of long speeches come short sayings of two lines, nearly all of which stand on their own. In chapters 10–15 the second line usually turns against the first ("A wise son makes a father glad, but a son who is a fool is his mother's grief", Proverbs 10:1). Some half-lines are used twice (Proverbs 10:2 and 11:4; 10:6 and 10:11; 10:8 and 10:10; 13:14 and 14:27), and one whole saying is repeated later (Proverbs 14:12 and 16:25), signs that the collectors drew on a shared stock of sayings. Proverbs 15:20 repeats the first line of 10:1, closing the first half of the collection.

sections.h: The wisest of women builds her house
sections.b: "The wisest of women builds her house, but folly tears it down with her own hands" (Proverbs 14:1). The saying sets the picture of Wisdom's house in Proverbs 9:1 in an ordinary home; many scholars re-point the Hebrew to read "Wisdom" itself. In Proverbs 10–15 wisdom is practical: it shows in work (Proverbs 10:5), in speech (Proverbs 10:19; 12:18), in taking correction (Proverbs 12:1; 13:1) and in choosing friends (Proverbs 13:20). Its root is the fear of the LORD, "wisdom's discipline" (Proverbs 15:33).

These chapters neither praise nor condemn wealth in itself. They note its power ("A rich man's wealth is a fortress town to him", Proverbs 10:15; Proverbs 14:20), credit it to the LORD's blessing and to hard work (Proverbs 10:4, 22), and warn that it is no help "on the day of fury" (Proverbs 11:4), that it can be faked (Proverbs 13:7), and that money gained quickly or dishonestly shrinks away (Proverbs 13:11). The "better than" sayings put it in its place: "A little, along with the fear of the LORD, is better than a big store of treasure with turmoil inside it" (Proverbs 15:16).

sections.b: Proverbs 10–15 sees poverty from two sides. Some sayings warn that laziness leads to want (Proverbs 10:4; 13:4). Others refuse to blame the poor: their fields could feed them, "but some are swept away where there is no justice" (Proverbs 13:23), and their neighbors abandon them (Proverbs 14:20). The strongest line grounds care for the poor in God himself: "Oppressing the poor is taunting the one who made them; showing kindness to the needy honors him" (Proverbs 14:31).
sections.refs: Proverbs 10:4; Proverbs 10:15; Proverbs 13:23; Proverbs 14:20–21; Proverbs 14:31; Proverbs 17:5; Matthew 25:40

sections.h: "No trouble at all will fall to the righteous man"
sections.b: Proverbs 10–15 states the link between deed and outcome more often and more boldly than any other part of the Bible. The righteous live long and are remembered with blessing; the wicked are cut short (Proverbs 10:7, 27). "No trouble at all will fall to the righteous man" (Proverbs 12:21). Many scholars read these as general truths meant to shape young people's habits, not as promises for every case; Job and Ecclesiastes test the same rule against cases that break it. The sayings also point beyond visible results: the righteous man "takes refuge in his death" (Proverbs 14:32), and the Greek of Proverbs 11:31 became, in 1 Peter 4:18, a word about the last judgment.
sections.refs: Proverbs 10:27; Proverbs 11:31; Proverbs 12:21; Proverbs 14:32; Job 21:7; Ecclesiastes 7:15; 1 Peter 4:18

sections.b: Proverbs 10–15 keeps the picture of two roads from chapters 1–9: the road of life that runs upward (Proverbs 15:24) and the roads that end in death. One saying, found twice in the book, warns that a person's own judgment cannot be trusted to tell them apart: "There is a road that looks straight to a person, but in the end it comes out on the roads of death" (Proverbs 14:12; 16:25). Proverbs 12:28 goes furthest: "On the road of righteousness there is life; and where its path goes, death is not."

sections.h: Four trees of life in Proverbs
sections.b: After Genesis, the "tree of life" appears in the Hebrew Bible only in Proverbs, four times: wisdom itself (Proverbs 3:18), the fruit of a righteous man (Proverbs 11:30), a longing that comes true (Proverbs 13:12) and a tongue that heals (Proverbs 15:4). In chapters 11–15 the phrase has become a picture of whatever gives and renews life. Jewish readers applied it to the Torah, and the Christian Bible ends with the tree restored in the new Jerusalem (Revelation 22:2).
sections.refs: Genesis 2:9; Genesis 3:22–24; Proverbs 3:18; Proverbs 11:30; Proverbs 13:12; Proverbs 15:4; Revelation 22:2

sections.b: "Sheol and Abaddon are in full view of the LORD; how much more the hearts of human beings!" (Proverbs 15:11). Even the world of the dead is open to God, so nothing in a person can be hidden from him. Proverbs 15:24 adds that the road of life "runs upward for one with good sense, to keep him away from Sheol down below"; in context this means escaping an early death, though later readers heard it of the life to come.

Proverbs 15:11 pairs Abaddon, "destruction", with Sheol as the deepest places in the world, both open to the LORD's sight (compare Job 26:6; Proverbs 27:20). In Revelation 9:11 Abaddon has become the name of the angel of the abyss.

Proverbs 15:8 echoes the prophets: "When the wicked sacrifice, the LORD finds it abhorrent; when the upright pray, he is pleased." The worth of worship depends on the worshiper's life (1 Samuel 15:22; Isaiah 1:11–17; Amos 5:21–24), and the prayer of the upright needs no offering to be welcome. The Damascus Document from Qumran quotes the verse, and in the Reformation era the Westminster Confession cited it on the works of the unregenerate (see justification).
sections.refs: Proverbs 15:8; Proverbs 15:29; Proverbs 21:3; Proverbs 21:27; 1 Samuel 15:22; Isaiah 1:11–17; Amos 5:21–24

sections.b: Because Proverbs 15:8 calls the sacrifice of the wicked abhorrent to the LORD, it was drawn into the Reformation debate about the good works of people who are not yet justified. The Westminster Confession (16.7) cites it to teach that such works, though good in themselves, are sinful before God; the Anglican Article 13 says they "have the nature of sin"; the Council of Trent denied that all works done before justification are sins. The chapter page for Proverbs 15 sets out the views.

"A woman of strength is her husband's crown, but one who shames him is like rot in his bones" (Proverbs 12:4). The phrase "woman of strength" ('eshet chayil) returns in the poem of Proverbs 31:10–31 and in Ruth 3:11. Proverbs 10–15 also praises the gracious woman (Proverbs 11:16) and the wisest of women, who builds her house (Proverbs 14:1), and warns against beauty without sense (Proverbs 11:22).
sections.refs: Proverbs 11:16; Proverbs 11:22; Proverbs 12:4; Proverbs 14:1; Proverbs 31:10; Ruth 3:11

sections.h: The king's glory is his people
sections.b: The first king sayings of the Solomon collection come at Proverbs 14:28–35. They measure a king by his people ("The more people there are, the more splendid the king", Proverbs 14:28), say that righteousness, not power, "raises a nation up" (Proverbs 14:34), and describe a king who rewards good sense and punishes disgrace in his servants (Proverbs 14:35). Many more follow in Proverbs 16:10–15.

The Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope teaches that poverty "in the hand of the god" is better than riches in the storehouse, and bread with a happy heart better than riches with vexation, close to Proverbs 15:16–17. It also forbids moving "the boundaries of a widow" (compare Proverbs 15:25) and altering scales and weights (compare Proverbs 11:1). Since Proverbs 22:17–24:22 clearly draws on Amenemope, these parallels may show that the same teaching was known to the sages of the Solomon collection.

Hesed in these chapters is a virtue people practice. "A person of loyal love does good to his own self" (Proverbs 11:17), and "loyal love and faithfulness are for those who plow up good" (Proverbs 14:22). The pair "loyal love and faithfulness", used of God in Exodus 34:6, is here the mark of a good neighbor.

Proverbs 10:2 and 11:4 share a half-line: "righteousness rescues from death". Jewish tradition, where tsedaqah came to mean charity, read it as a promise to those who give to the poor (Bavli Shabbat 156b). Proverbs 11:24–26 adds that the one who gives freely ends up with more, that "the one who gives others water will get a drink himself", and that the one who hoards grain in a famine is cursed. Paul uses the same logic in 2 Corinthians 9:6–9.

"Whoever keeps back his rod hates his son, but one who loves him seeks him out early with discipline" (Proverbs 13:24). This is the first of the rod sayings that run through the Solomon collections (Proverbs 22:15; 23:13–14; 29:15). The verse argues that neglect is a failure of love, and it assumes the physical punishment that was normal in the ancient world. "Spare the rod and spoil the child" is not in the Bible; it is best known in this form from Samuel Butler's poem Hudibras (1664), though the proverb is older. The chapter page for Proverbs 13 sets out how Jewish and Christian readers have used and limited the verse, and how it is read today.

sections.b: No subject fills Proverbs 10–15 more than speech. The mouth of the righteous is "a spring of life" (Proverbs 10:11), while many words lead to wrongdoing (Proverbs 10:19). Words can wound or heal: "Some people blurt words that stab like a sword, but the tongue of the wise is a cure" (Proverbs 12:18), and "A tongue that heals is a tree of life" (Proverbs 15:4). The gossip betrays confidences (Proverbs 11:13), the false witness lies (Proverbs 12:17; 14:5, 25), and the best-known saying of all teaches the power of a gentle reply: "A soft-spoken answer turns fury back, but a hurtful word makes anger climb" (Proverbs 15:1).
sections.refs: Proverbs 10:11; Proverbs 10:19; Proverbs 11:13; Proverbs 12:17–19; Proverbs 15:1; Proverbs 15:4; James 3:5–8

sections.b: Proverbs 10–15 sets the hard worker against the lazy one again and again. "A slack hand at work leaves a person poor, but the hand of hard workers brings riches" (Proverbs 10:4). The son who brings the harvest in on time has good sense (Proverbs 10:5); the lazy messenger is like vinegar to teeth and smoke to eyes (Proverbs 10:26); "Every kind of toil brings some gain, but lip-talk ends up only in want" (Proverbs 14:23). Yet work is not everything: "It is the LORD's blessing that makes a person rich, and toil adds nothing to it" (Proverbs 10:22).

sections.b: Two sayings in Proverbs 10–15 have been read as hints of life beyond death. Proverbs 12:28 ends, in the Hebrew, "where its path goes, death is not", and Proverbs 14:32 says "the righteous man takes refuge in his death". Many scholars think both mean only that the righteous escape an untimely death; the Greek of Proverbs 14:32 reads "in his holiness" instead of "in his death". Others, with many Jewish and Christian readers, hear in them a hope that reaches past the grave.

Proverbs 15 twice sets prayer against the wicked's religion: "when the upright pray, he is pleased" (Proverbs 15:8), and "The LORD keeps far away from the wicked, but the prayers of the righteous he hears" (Proverbs 15:29). Prayer is welcome where sacrifice from a wicked life is not.

"The LORD pulls up the house of the proud, but he makes the widow's boundary stone stand" (Proverbs 15:25). A widow without sons had no one to stop a neighbor from moving the stones that marked her family's field. Israel's law cursed anyone who moved a boundary stone (Deuteronomy 19:14; Deuteronomy 27:17), and Proverbs makes the LORD himself the widow's defender (compare Proverbs 23:10–11).

sections.h: "In every place the LORD has his eyes open"
sections.b: The sayings of Proverbs 10–15 are set inside a picture of a God who sees and governs. "In every place the LORD has his eyes open, on the lookout over evil people and good" (Proverbs 15:3); Sheol and Abaddon and the human heart lie open before him (Proverbs 15:11). He will not leave the righteous to starve (Proverbs 10:3), favors the good and condemns the schemer (Proverbs 12:2), and defends the widow (Proverbs 15:25).

sections.b: Proverbs 11:15 warns against guaranteeing an outsider's debt: "Stand good for an outsider's loan, and you will be badly hurt; hate the handshake that seals a pledge, and you are safe." The same warning comes at Proverbs 6:1–5, 17:18, 20:16, 22:26–27 and 27:13. A guarantor who could not pay might lose his land, his bed or his freedom.
